components.note: 心 (heart) — 恐 describes fear felt in the heart.
巩 (gǒng) gives a sound close to kǒng, sharing the same rhyme.
忄 (heart) shows 惧 relates to an emotion.
具 (jù) gives the exact sound of 惧.

example.hanzi: 她克服了对失败的恐惧。
example.pinyin: Tā kèfú le duì shībài de kǒngjù.
example.english: She overcame her fear of failure.
example.fact: 恐惧 doubles up two "heart" radicals — 心 in 恐, 忄 in 惧 — fitting for a formal, written-register word for deep dread; everyday spoken Chinese reaches for the plainer 怕 instead ("我怕黑" rather than the more literary "我对黑暗感到恐惧").

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谈 relates to talking, conversation
炎 (yán) gives a sound close to 谈's reading tán
讠 (speech) — 论 relates to discussing or explaining something with words.
仑 (logical order, arrangement) — combined with speech, 论 came to mean 'to discuss' or 'a theory,' explaining ideas in an orderly way.

example.hanzi: 我们在谈论明天的计划。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài tánlùn míngtiān de jìhuà.
example.english: We are discussing tomorrow's plan.
example.fact: 谈论 is a transitive verb that takes its topic directly as an object — 谈论这个问题 ("discuss this issue") — with no preposition needed, unlike English "talk about," where "about" can't simply be dropped.

components.note: 令 (an order, command) — 命 pictures issuing a command.
口 (mouth) — a command given aloud gave 命 its meaning 'order' or 'decree,' and by extension, 'fate' or 'life.'
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 运's meaning 'to move, transport,' and by extension 'fortune,' the movement of one's life.
云 (yún) gives a sound hint — 运 is pronounced yùn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 他相信自己能改变命运。
example.pinyin: Tā xiāngxìn zìjǐ néng gǎibiàn mìngyùn.
example.english: He believes he can change his own fate.
example.fact: 运 alone already means "luck, fortune" (as in 幸运, "lucky"), while 命 separately means "life, decree" — 命运 fuses a person's "life-decree" with "fortune" into one grander idea of overarching destiny, bigger in scope than the everyday luck of 运气.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
纟 (thread) — 组 originally meant 'to weave, arrange,' extended to 'group, to organize.'
且 (qiě) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zǔ.

example.hanzi: 老师把学生分成了五个小组。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī bǎ xuésheng fēnchéng le wǔ gè xiǎozǔ.
example.english: The teacher divided the students into five groups.
example.fact: 组 carries the silk-thread radical 纟 because it originally meant "to weave, to arrange" — the same image of interlacing strands behind 组织 ("organization"), with 小组 simply naming a smaller such unit inside a larger body.

components.note: 弓 (bow) — the weapon being drawn.
丨 depicts the taut drawstring being pulled back — giving 引 its meaning 'to pull, draw out, attract.'
走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.

example.hanzi: 这个消息引起了很多人的注意。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi yǐnqǐ le hěn duō rén de zhùyì.
example.english: This news drew a lot of people's attention.
example.fact: 引起 almost always takes an abstract noun as its object — attention (注意), interest (兴趣), controversy (争议) — rather than a concrete physical event; for a plainer physical cause-and-effect, Chinese reaches for 导致 or 造成 instead, both of which lean more negative in tone.

components.note: 尸 (here representing a covering or stall, not a corpse) — 展 pictures a place where goods are displayed.
衣 (clothing) — clothing laid out for display gave 展 its meaning 'to unfold' or 'to exhibit.'

example.hanzi: 这个城市这些年发展得很快。
example.pinyin: Zhège chéngshì zhèxiē nián fāzhǎn de hěn kuài.
example.english: This city has developed very quickly in recent years.
example.fact: 展 alone already means "to unfold, to spread out" (built from the image of clothing laid out for display, 尸+衣) — 发展 literally combines "to send forth" with "to unfold," a vivid image of outward expansion that maps neatly onto its modern sense of economic or personal "development."

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 每个水分子都由两个氢原子和一个氧原子组成。
example.pinyin: Měi gè shuǐ fēnzǐ dōu yóu liǎng gè qīng yuánzǐ hé yí gè yǎng yuánzǐ zǔchéng.
example.english: Every water molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
example.fact: 分子 has two separate CEDICT readings for the same two characters: fēnzǐ, "molecule" (or "numerator" in math), is the ordinary standalone reading, while fènzǐ, "a member of a group," surfaces only bound inside words like 恐怖分子 ("terrorist") and 知识分子 ("intellectual") — easy to conflate since the characters and tones look almost identical on the page.

components.note: Originally depicted a burning candle or the sun's rays radiating outward — the source of 白's meaning 'white, bright, clear.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 那个白人男子是我们的新老师。
example.pinyin: Nàge báirén nánzǐ shì wǒmen de xīn lǎoshī.
example.english: That white man is our new teacher.
example.fact: 白人 follows a simple, transparent pattern shared by 黑人 ("Black person") and 亚洲人 ("Asian person") — colour or origin term plus 人 ("person") — one of Mandarin's most predictable ways to name an ethnicity.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惊 relates to an emotional reaction of shock or fright
京 (jīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 惊's reading jīng
讠 (speech) — 讶 describes an exclamation of surprise.
牙 (yá) gives the sound — an exact match with 讶, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,他感到非常惊讶。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā gǎndào fēicháng jīngyà.
example.english: Hearing this news, he felt very astonished.
example.fact: Both characters point to a physical reaction — 惊 carries the heart radical 忄 for an emotional jolt, and 讶 carries the speech radical 讠 for the exclamation that jolt produces — together painting astonishment as something felt in the chest and voiced aloud.

components.note: A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 桌子上放着一本书。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng fàngzhe yì běn shū.
example.english: There's a book lying on the table.
example.fact: 子 here is a fully "bleached" noun suffix — it contributes no meaning of its own (unlike in 孩子, where 子 still echoes "child") and simply marks 桌 as a countable, concrete noun, the same grammatical role it plays in 椅子 ("chair") and 杯子 ("cup").

components.note: 十 here relates to completeness, since 十 (ten) is a round, whole number.
比 (bǐ) gives a sound distantly related to bì, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她今年夏天从大学毕业。
example.pinyin: Tā jīnnián xiàtiān cóng dàxué bìyè.
example.english: She will graduate from university this summer.
example.fact: 毕业 is a verb-object compound built from 毕 ("to finish") plus 业 ("course of study") — literally "to finish one's studies" — which is why it's grammatically intransitive: you say 从大学毕业 ("graduate from university"), never 毕业大学.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 练 originally meant to boil and whiten silk thread, extending to 'to practice, to train' through repeated refinement.
柬 (jiǎn) gives a sound distantly related to liàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 我每天都练习写汉字。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān dōu liànxí xiě Hànzì.
example.english: I practice writing Chinese characters every day.
example.fact: 练 alone traces back to boiling and whitening raw silk thread until it becomes smooth and refined — 练习 extends that image of repeated refinement to any skill honed through repetition, from a musical instrument to a foreign language.

components.note: 黑 pictures a face or window blackened by soot rising from a fire 灬 below — giving 黑 its meaning 'black, dark.'
日 (sun) — 暗 describes the absence of light, the opposite of a bright sun.
音 (yīn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading àn has diverged.

example.hanzi: 夜晚的森林一片黑暗。
example.pinyin: Yèwǎn de sēnlín yí piàn hēi'àn.
example.english: The forest at night is pitch dark.
example.fact: 黑暗 doubles up two independent "dark" characters — 黑 (soot blackening a face over a fire) and 暗 (the sun 日 obscured) — and unlike the more physical 黑 alone, 黑暗 extends naturally into a figurative "dark" as well, as in 黑暗的时代 ("a dark age").

components.note: 木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.
土 (earth) — 场 relates to a flat open area of ground, such as a field or venue.
昜 (yáng) gives a hint of the sound — 场 is pronounced chǎng, a connection that has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 我们明天早上八点到机场。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān zǎoshang bā diǎn dào jīchǎng.
example.english: We'll arrive at the airport at eight tomorrow morning.
example.fact: 场 (a flat open area of ground, from 土 "earth") is Mandarin's general term for a large purpose-built venue — the same character turns up in 广场 ("public square") and 停车场 ("parking lot") — with 机场 simply naming the "ground" set aside for aircraft (机).

meanings: publicly funded institution, enterprise or foundation

example.hanzi: 他把所有的时间都花在了事业上。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ suǒyǒu de shíjiān dōu huā zài le shìyè shàng.
example.english: He spends all his time on his career.
example.fact: 事业 sits a notch grander than the everyday word for "job" — 工作 covers any ordinary employment, while 事业 implies a larger, meaningful undertaking or life's work, closer to English "career" or "cause" than a mere day job.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
An altered form of 囟 (the mind/head) — the seat of thought.
心 (heart) — thinking was pictured as an activity of both mind and heart, giving 思 its meaning 'to think.'
讠 (speech) — relates to 议's meaning 'to discuss, deliberate; opinion.'
义 (yì) gives the sound — 议 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这个魔术表演真是不可思议。
example.pinyin: Zhège móshù biǎoyǎn zhēnshi bùkěsīyì.
example.english: This magic performance is truly incredible.
example.fact: 不可思议 is often traced to Buddhist sutra translation, where it rendered a Sanskrit term for a truth beyond ordinary conception — thought (思) and discourse (议) alike fall short of grasping it. The everyday modern sense, "unbelievable, incredible," is a secularized descendant of that religious original.

components.note: 父 (father) — 爷 belongs to the family of words for male elders.
耶 (yé) gives the sound — an exact match with 爷's reading yé.
父 (father) — 爷 belongs to the family of words for male elders.
耶 (yé) gives the sound — an exact match with 爷's reading yé.

example.hanzi: 爷爷每天早上都去公园散步。
example.pinyin: Yéye měitiān zǎoshang dōu qù gōngyuán sànbù.
example.english: Grandpa goes for a walk in the park every morning.
example.fact: Chinese kinship terms distinguish sides of the family where English doesn't: 爷爷 is specifically the father's father, while the mother's father is 外公 — the "outer" 外 marking the maternal side as literally "outside" the family line.

components.note: 人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.hanzi: 你等我一会儿,我马上就来。
example.pinyin: Nǐ děng wǒ yíhuìr, wǒ mǎshàng jiù lái.
example.english: Wait for me a moment, I'll come right away.
example.fact: 会儿 almost never stands alone — it's the second half of set phrases like 一会儿 ("in a moment") and 这会儿 ("right now"), and its r-suffix (儿化) marks it as northern, colloquial Mandarin; more formal writing tends to avoid it.

components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
弋 (an awl or tool) — one of the craftsman's instruments.
工 (a measuring square) — a tool for making things to a fixed pattern, giving 式 its meaning 'style, form, type.'

example.hanzi: 会议将在下周正式开始。
example.pinyin: Huìyì jiāng zài xià zhōu zhèngshì kāishǐ.
example.english: The meeting will officially begin next week.
example.fact: 正式 pairs a "correct, proper" root (正) with a "style, pattern" root (式) — together, "conforming to the proper pattern." Its antonym 非正式 ("informal") simply negates the same compound with 非 rather than swapping in an unrelated word, a common pattern in Chinese antonym formation.

components.note: 厂 (a building) — 厨 names a room in a building, the kitchen.
豆 (dòu) gives a sound distantly related to 厨's reading chú, having drifted apart over time.
户 (door) — 房 relates to a room or house, a space behind a door
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 房 is pronounced fáng, a close match

example.hanzi: 妈妈在厨房里做饭。
example.pinyin: Māma zài chúfáng lǐ zuòfàn.
example.english: Mom is cooking in the kitchen.
example.fact: 房 is Mandarin's general word for a room within a building (卧房 "bedroom," 书房 "study"), and 厨 narrows it specifically to cooking — the same transparent "room for X" logic runs through most Chinese words for rooms.

components.note: 牛 (ox) — 特 originally referred to a male ox singled out for sacrifice, a special animal set apart from the herd.
寺 (sì) gives a hint of the sound — 特 is pronounced tè, a connection that has drifted over time.
歹 (bad, death) — 殊 originally related to death or being cut off, extended to mean 'set apart, different.'
朱 (zhū) gives a sound close to shū.

example.hanzi: 这是一个特殊的情况,我们需要特别处理。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè tèshū de qíngkuàng, wǒmen xūyào tèbié chǔlǐ.
example.english: This is a special situation; we need to handle it specially.
example.fact: 特 traces back to a male ox singled out for ritual sacrifice, set apart from the rest of the herd — an image of being "picked out" that survives abstractly in both 特殊 ("out of the ordinary") and 特别 ("especially"), built on the same root.

example.hanzi: 你在大学学的是什么专业?
example.pinyin: Nǐ zài dàxué xué de shì shénme zhuānyè?
example.english: What was your major in university?
example.fact: 专业 does double duty as both a noun ("major, specialized field") and an adjective ("professional, expert") — 他很专业 ("He's very professional") uses the same two characters as 我的专业 ("my major"), with word class inferred purely from position in the sentence.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.

example.hanzi: 他是一个很老实的人,从不说谎。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè hěn lǎoshi de rén, cóngbù shuōhuǎng.
example.english: He's a very honest person who never lies.
example.fact: 老实 can flip from a compliment to a mild criticism depending on context — praising someone's honesty in one sentence, or gently mocking their naivety in the next (老实人 often implies someone too trusting for their own good) — a duality English "honest" doesn't carry.

components.note: 日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'
饣 (food) — 饭 names cooked rice, a meal.
反 (fǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 饭.

example.hanzi: 我们一家人一起吃晚饭。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yì jiā rén yìqǐ chī wǎnfàn.
example.english: Our whole family eats dinner together.
example.fact: 饭 literally means "cooked rice" before it means "meal" in general — 晚饭 ("evening rice"), 早饭 ("morning rice"), and 午饭 ("noon rice") all build on that same core word, a linguistic fossil of rice's central place in a traditional Chinese meal.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吸 describes breathing in through the mouth.
及 (jí) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xī has diverged.
弓 (bow) — the weapon being drawn.
丨 depicts the taut drawstring being pulled back — giving 引 its meaning 'to pull, draw out, attract.'

example.hanzi: 这家博物馆吸引了很多游客。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā bówùguǎn xīyǐn le hěn duō yóukè.
example.english: This museum attracts many tourists.
example.fact: 吸 (built around 口, "mouth") originally described breathing in air, and 引 (a bow 弓 with its string 丨 drawn back) meant "to pull" — 吸引 fuses "inhaling" and "pulling toward" into one vivid image of drawing something in.

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'
亻 (person) — 代 relates to a person's place in time.
弋 (a stake used to mark or catch something) — combined with 亻 (person), 代 came to mean a 'generation' or 'era,' and 'to take the place of' someone.

example.hanzi: 这首歌是八十年代的经典。
example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu gē shì bāshí niándài de jīngdiǎn.
example.english: This song is a classic from the eighties.
example.fact: 年代 has a distinctive use for naming a decade of a century — 八十年代 means "the eighties (1980s)," not "eighty years" — a construction that trips up learners used to English's simpler "the 80s."

components.note: 八 (two hands) — gripping the weapon.
丘 (an axe/weapon) — held with both hands, the image of a person bearing arms giving 兵 its meaning 'soldier, weapon, military.'

example.hanzi: 这些士兵已经在边境驻守了三年。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē shìbīng yǐjīng zài biānjìng zhùshǒu le sān nián.
example.english: These soldiers have been stationed at the border for three years.
example.fact: 兵 pictures hands gripping a weapon, and its root sense spans both "weapon" and the person who wields one — a double sense still visible in 兵器 ("weaponry") next to 士兵 ("soldier"), where the same character can point either to the gear or to the person carrying it.

meanings: since (used after a specified time or event)

components.note: Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 自从他搬来这里以来,我们成了好朋友。
example.pinyin: Zìcóng tā bān lái zhèlǐ yǐlái, wǒmen chéng le hǎo péngyou.
example.english: Ever since he moved here, we've become good friends.
example.fact: 以来 always looks backward from a past point up to the present, and pairs naturally with 自从 ("ever since") at the front of the clause — it can't be used the way English sometimes stretches "since" toward the future.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 今天天气很好,我的心情也不错。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān tiānqì hěn hǎo, wǒ de xīnqíng yě búcuò.
example.english: The weather is nice today, and I'm in a good mood too.
example.fact: 心情 names a mood or momentary emotional state, distinct from 性格 ("personality," a lasting trait) — a useful trio to keep straight alongside 感情 ("feelings, an emotional bond between people"), each covering a different slice of "how someone feels."

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching out to try to catch something.
隹 (a bird) — catching a bird by hand is hard, giving 难 its meaning 'difficult.'
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 听到这个坏消息,她很难过。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège huài xiāoxi, tā hěn nánguò.
example.english: Hearing this bad news, she felt very sad.
example.fact: 难过 literally means "hard to get through" (难 "difficult" + 过 "to pass, to cross") — the same logic behind 好过 ("easy to get through, comfortable") — turning a physical image of crossing rough terrain into an emotional description of sadness or hardship.

components.note: 尸, here a variant of 厂, depicts a roof or shelter.
至 depicts arriving or coming to rest — settling under a roof gave 屋 its meaning 'house, room.'
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 这个屋子太小了,放不下这张床。
example.pinyin: Zhège wūzi tài xiǎo le, fàng bu xià zhè zhāng chuáng.
example.english: This room is too small to fit this bed.
example.fact: 屋子 and 房间 are near-synonyms for "room," but 屋子 leans more colloquial and spoken while 房间 feels a touch more neutral or formal — a register distinction that rarely survives translation into a single English word "room."

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 制 relates to cutting and shaping, and by extension, to making or controlling something.
巾 (jīn) gives a hint of the sound — 制 is pronounced zhì, a connection that has drifted over time.
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 造's meaning 'to make, build,' an action carried through to completion.
告 (gào) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zào.

example.hanzi: 这家工厂制造汽车零件。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngchǎng zhìzào qìchē língjiàn.
example.english: This factory manufactures car parts.
example.fact: 制造 is reserved for tangible, industrial production — cars, machines, weapons — while the near-synonym 制作 covers smaller-scale or artisanal making (a film, a handicraft, a meal); mixing the two is a common slip since English "make" covers both without distinction.

components.note: 入 (enter, put away) — 全 pictures something being placed into safekeeping.
玉 (jade) — a valuable treasure kept whole and undamaged, giving 全 its meaning of 'complete' or 'entire.'
阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning city/settlement) — 都 relates to a capital or metropolis.
者 (zhě) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches dōu, reflecting centuries of sound change.

example.hanzi: 我说的话他们全都记住了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ shuō de huà tāmen quándōu jìzhù le.
example.english: They remembered everything I said, without exception.
example.fact: 全都 stacks two words that each already mean roughly "all" on their own — 全 ("entire, whole") and 都 ("all, each") — for emphasis; despite the doubling, native speakers don't feel it as redundant the way an English speaker might feel about saying "all entirely."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
贝 (money) — gambling involves staking money.
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to dǔ, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 我跟你打赌,他一定会来。
example.pinyin: Wǒ gēn nǐ dǎdǔ, tā yídìng huì lái.
example.english: I bet you, he will definitely come.
example.fact: 打 is one of Mandarin's most flexible "light verbs," combining with dozens of otherwise unrelated nouns to form new verbs with little literal connection to "hit" — 打赌 ("to bet"), 打电话 ("to make a phone call"), and 打扫 ("to clean") all lean on the same all-purpose 打.

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.hanzi: 他坐在我和她中间。
example.pinyin: Tā zuò zài wǒ hé tā zhōngjiān.
example.english: He sits between me and her.
example.fact: 中间 nearly always follows the noun(s) it locates rather than preceding them — 我们中间 ("among us"), 两者中间 ("between the two") — the reverse of English "between us," a pattern shared by most Chinese words of relative position (上面, 下面, 里面).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唱 describes singing, an action made with the mouth.
昌 (chāng) gives a sound close to chàng, differing only in tone.
欠 (breath, an open mouth exhaling) — 歌 relates to the breath used in singing.
哥 (gē) gives the sound — an exact match with 歌's reading gē.

example.hanzi: 她喜欢在洗澡的时候唱歌。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zài xǐzǎo de shíhou chànggē.
example.english: She likes to sing while showering.
example.fact: 唱歌 is a verb-object compound that's already grammatically complete on its own — to specify what song, Chinese has to reinsert an object around it (唱一首歌, "sing a song"; 唱这首歌, "sing this song"), since 歌 is already used up inside the fixed verb phrase.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伦 relates to human relationships and social order.
仑 depicts an orderly, logical arrangement — combined with 亻, giving 伦 its meaning 'human relationships, order.'
Offering/enjoying — links to the idea of sincere giving.
Gives a sound distantly related to dūn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她去年搬到伦敦工作了。
example.pinyin: Tā qùnián bān dào Lúndūn gōngzuò le.
example.english: She moved to London to work last year.
example.fact: 伦敦 is a straightforward sound-based transliteration of "London," with no attempt at meaningful characters — unlike place names that mix sound and sense, both 伦 and 敦 were chosen purely for how closely they approximate the English syllables.

components.note: 牛 (ox) — 特 originally referred to a male ox singled out for sacrifice, a special animal set apart from the herd.
寺 (sì) gives a hint of the sound — 特 is pronounced tè, a connection that has drifted over time.
工 depicts a carpenter's square or workman's tool — a simple shape that came to represent work and labor.

example.hanzi: 电影里的那个特工成功地完成了任务。
example.pinyin: Diànyǐng lǐ de nàge tègōng chénggōng de wánchéng le rènwu.
example.english: The secret agent in the movie successfully completed the mission.
example.fact: 特工 pairs the "special, set apart" root 特 (also seen in 特殊, elsewhere in this batch) with 工 ("work") — literally "special-duty work[er]" — much as the near-synonym 特务 ("special affairs") compresses to the same core meaning, "secret agent."

components.note: 亻 (person) — 停 relates to a person coming to a halt
亭 (tíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 停's reading tíng
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 这里不可以停车。
example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ bù kěyǐ tíngchē.
example.english: You can't park here.
example.fact: 停车 is a fixed verb-object compound (停 "to stop" + 车 "vehicle"), so naming a location often means putting it before the verb rather than tacking it on after, as English does — 在路边停车 ("park by the roadside"), literally "at the roadside, stop-vehicle."

components.note: 戈 (a spear) in the center is the weapon being wielded.
廾 (two hands) surrounding it show hands gripping the weapon on guard, giving 戒 its meaning 'to guard against, to warn.'
扌 (hand) — 指 relates to using the hand, specifically the fingers.
旨 (an aim, purpose) — combined with 扌 (hand), 指 came to mean 'finger' and 'to point,' aiming the hand at something.

example.hanzi: 他送给她一枚戒指作为生日礼物。
example.pinyin: Tā sòng gěi tā yì méi jièzhi zuòwéi shēngrì lǐwù.
example.english: He gave her a ring as a birthday present.
example.fact: 戒 by itself means "to guard against, to give up (a habit)," as in 戒烟 ("to quit smoking") — only in the compound 戒指 does it take on the narrower sense of a finger ring, which one popular explanation traces to a reminder-band once meant to "guard" the wearer against forgetting a vow or warning.

components.note: 回 depicts a spiral or winding shape — something that turns back on itself, giving rise to the meaning 'to return.'
大 (big) — in 头's simplified form, this element is linked to the idea of 'high' or topmost, since the head sits at the top of the body.

example.hanzi: 她听到有人叫她,回头看了一下。
example.pinyin: Tā tīngdào yǒurén jiào tā, huítóu kàn le yíxià.
example.english: She heard someone call her and turned her head to look.
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense of turning one's head, 回头 has drifted into a common colloquial way of saying "later" (回头再说, "let's talk about it later") — the same shift from a physical action to an abstract time reference behind English "in a bit," literally a small piece, meaning "soon."

components.note: 礻 (altar, spirit) on the left sets a religious scene.
兄 (a person, shown here kneeling or speaking) on the right shows someone praying, giving 祝 its meaning 'to wish, to pray for blessings.'
加 (to add) on top shows the act of contributing.
贝 (money, fortune) below is what's being added to, giving 贺 its meaning 'to congratulate' – originally offering a gift to add to someone's good fortune.

example.hanzi: 我要祝贺你顺利通过考试。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yào zhùhè nǐ shùnlì tōngguò kǎoshì.
example.english: I want to congratulate you on passing the exam successfully.
example.fact: 贺 alone traces back to adding (加) something valuable (贝, "money, shell currency") onto someone's good fortune — a literal gift piled onto their luck — which is why 祝贺 pairs naturally with an occasion worth celebrating (毕业, 生日, 结婚) rather than casual good news.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 案 originally referred to a wooden table or desk
安 (ān) gives a sound close to 案's reading àn, differing only in tone
亻 (person) — 件 relates to a person separating something into parts.
牛 (ox) — dividing an ox into pieces gave 件 its meaning of an individual 'item' or 'piece,' now used as a measure word for objects and matters.

example.hanzi: 警察正在调查这起案件。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ ànjiàn.
example.english: The police are investigating this case.
example.fact: 案件 is reserved for a legal or criminal matter under investigation — a police case, a court case — and would sound strange applied to an everyday "case" as in "in that case," which Chinese instead expresses with an entirely different word, 情况 or 如果.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 件 relates to a person separating something into parts.
牛 (ox) — dividing an ox into pieces gave 件 its meaning of an individual 'item' or 'piece,' now used as a measure word for objects and matters.

example.hanzi: 他答应了,但提出了一个条件。
example.pinyin: Tā dāying le, dàn tíchū le yí gè tiáojiàn.
example.english: He agreed, but put forward one condition.
example.fact: 条件 shares its second character 件 with 案件 (also in this batch) — 件 works as a measure word for discrete items and matters, so both words literally count off individual, itemized "pieces" of something, whether legal cases or the separate stipulations of an agreement.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.
口 (mouth), stacked three times — many mouths talking about or judging something, the source of 品's meaning 'product, item; quality, rank.'

example.hanzi: 这是她最有名的一部作品。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì tā zuì yǒumíng de yí bù zuòpǐn.
example.english: This is her most famous work.
example.fact: 品, tripling the mouth radical 口, originally suggested many people tasting, judging, or ranking something — 作品 ("a work that's been made") keeps a faint trace of that sense, a finished piece put up for others to judge and appraise.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.hanzi: 他手里拿着一本书。
example.pinyin: Tā shǒulǐ ná zhe yì běn shū.
example.english: He's holding a book in his hand.
example.fact: 手里 extends beyond the literal hand to mean "in someone's control or possession" — 钱在他手里 ("the money is in his hands," i.e. under his control) — the same metaphor English uses when it says a decision is "in someone's hands."

components.note: 冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 他们在大学的时候爱上了对方。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài dàxué de shíhou àishàng le duìfāng.
example.english: They fell in love with each other in university.
example.fact: 上 tacked onto a verb often marks the moment an action successfully "sticks" or takes hold — 爱上 ("fall in love with"), 看上 ("take a liking to"), 迷上 ("become obsessed with") — a small but very productive verb-complement pattern worth learning as a set.

components.note: Wood — shelves and frames were made of wood.
Gives the sound dāng, related to dàng but drifted apart over time.
木 (wood) — 案 originally referred to a wooden table or desk
安 (ān) gives a sound close to 案's reading àn, differing only in tone

example.hanzi: 这些档案都保存在地下室里。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē dàng'àn dōu bǎocún zài dìxiàshì lǐ.
example.english: These files are all kept in the basement.
example.fact: 档案 shares its second character 案 with 案件 (also in this batch) — both trace back to 案's original sense of a wooden table or desk, the surface where documents were once laid out, filed, and reviewed.

example.hanzi: 你千万不要告诉他这个秘密。
example.pinyin: Nǐ qiānwàn bú yào gàosu tā zhège mìmì.
example.english: Whatever you do, don't tell him this secret.
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense "ten million," 千万 has a second, seemingly unrelated use as an emphatic adverb meaning "whatever you do" — almost always paired with a negative command (千万不要..., "whatever you do, don't...") to add urgency to a warning.

components.note: 世 depicts three leaves or shoots on a stem, suggesting continuous growth across generations — giving rise to the meaning 'generation' or 'world.'

example.hanzi: 他的祖父去年去世了。
example.pinyin: Tā de zǔfù qùnián qùshì le.
example.english: His grandfather passed away last year.
example.fact: 去世 is a polite, formal euphemism for dying — literally "to leave the world" — sitting alongside other registers for death in Chinese, from the blunt 死 to the more elevated 逝世 reserved for public figures, each carrying a different degree of formality and respect.
